content.title: THE KITCHEN HABITS QUIETLY DESTROYING YOUR {{HEALTHY}} MEALS
facts: **Overcrowding the pan** – Too many vegetables at once steam instead of sear, which means they leach out water-soluble nutrients into the liquid pooling at the bottom instead of caramelizing.
**Boiling vegetables** – Broccoli and spinach can lose a large share of their vitamin C and B vitamins into the cooking water; steaming or microwaving keeps far more intact.
**Draining and tossing pasta/rice water** – That starchy water holds minerals and can be saved to thicken sauces, but most people pour it straight down the drain.
**Adding salt too early** – Salting watery vegetables like zucchini or eggplant too soon pulls out moisture before they even hit the heat, leaving you with soggy, steamed results instead of browned.
**Skipping the resting step** – Cutting into meat or fish right off the heat lets all the juices run out onto the plate instead of redistributing back into the fibers.
**Using the wrong oil for high heat** – Cooking extra virgin olive oil or flaxseed oil at high temperatures breaks it down and creates compounds you don't want; save those for finishing, not searing.
**Washing produce after cutting** – Slicing fruit before rinsing it can push surface bacteria into the flesh; always wash whole, then cut.
**Microwaving in the wrong container** – Reheating in certain plastic containers at high heat can leach compounds into food; glass or ceramic is the safer default.

content.caption:
A few of these kitchen habits are worth slowing down on. Take boiling vegetables: when broccoli or spinach hit rolling water, their water-soluble vitamins (like vitamin C and folate) actually dissolve out into the liquid, so you're pouring nutrients down the drain along with the water. Overcrowding the pan is another sneaky one — when there's too much food packed in, the temperature drops and everything releases steam instead of browning, which not only kills flavor but means less of those beneficial plant compounds get activated through proper searing. And skipping the resting step after cooking meat matters more than people think: cutting too soon lets the juices (and the nutrients carried in them) spill onto the cutting board instead of soaking back into the fibers. Everyone's kitchen setup is different, so adjust what makes sense for how you actually cook.
